title: Set head blocks snug against both sides of a casualty's head without moving it
instruction: The training casualty lies on a spine board and its head must not move. Stand one orange head block upright on the board at each side of the head, with its long side snug against the head, without pushing the head, then let go of both blocks.
context: Emergency medical care: in spinal motion restriction, once a casualty is on a long spine board or scoop stretcher, a rescuer keeps the head in line by hand until foam head blocks are placed snug against both sides of it and strapped. The head must not be pushed sideways, lifted or turned while the blocks go on, and a block left short of the head lets it roll. Taught in EMT and first-responder courses and done by emergency medical technicians and paramedics (O*NET 29-2042.00, 29-2043.00) and firefighters (33-2011.00). Here the trainer's head is a free weighted part: a block pushed hard against it shoves it off its marks, and a block stopped short leaves a gap, so each block must be brought to touching distance and set down gently, one on each side of the head.
setup: Bimanual YAM station; the table top is the reference height. x points forward from the line through the two arm bases, y to the left of the midpoint between them, z up from the table top; the arm bases are at y +30.5 cm and y -30.5 cm. Three kinds of thing are on the table. (1) Spine board: a yellow rigid high-density polyethylene board, 480 x 300 mm and 15 mm thick (480 mm along x), fixed to the table from x 12.0 to 60.0 cm, centred on y 0; its top is 15 mm above the table. (2) Casualty trainer, painted tan, lying on its back on the board with its head toward the arms. Its torso (a wooden block 300 mm along x, 200 mm wide, 50 mm tall, from x 30.0 to 60.0 cm) and neck (a wooden block 30 mm along x, 60 mm wide, 30 mm tall, from x 27.0 to 30.0 cm), both centred on y 0, are screwed to the board and cannot move. The head is a separate part: a tan PLA cylinder 120 mm across and 100 mm tall (back of the head to the face), weighted to 300 g, standing on one flat end on the board (axis vertical, back of the head down), centred at x 20.0 cm, y 0, so it spans x 14.0 to 26.0 cm and stops 10 mm short of the neck. Nothing holds it: any push moves it. Tape marks on the board around it show its starting place. (3) Two head blocks: orange closed-cell foam blocks with a vinyl cover, 70 x 50 mm and 80 mm tall, 40 g each, standing upright on the table beside the board with their 70 mm sides along x, centred at x 20.0 cm, y +28.0 cm and y -28.0 cm (one in front of each arm). Nothing else is on the table.
scoring: The score is read at the last step from the poses of the head and the two blocks, together with how far the head moved during the trial; the scorer also reads, from the embodiment's state, each gripper's tool point, finger-tip point (between the tips) and opening (0 closed, 1 fully open with the fingers 94 mm apart). The head's start is where its centre stood at the first step (x 20.0 cm, y 0). Seen from above, the head's outline is its 120 mm circle (for a tilted head, its axis seen from above widened by 60 mm) and a block's outline is the shadow of its corners. A block's 'gap' is the horizontal distance between its outline and the head's (0 or less where they touch). A block is on the side of the head its centre is on. A gripper has 'let go' of a block when its opening is 0.9 or more (fingers at least 84.5 mm apart) or its 'finger zone' is more than 10 mm from the block; the finger zone is every point within a radius of the segment from its finger-tip point to 38 mm back up the gripper, the radius reaching a finger's outer corner (half the finger gap plus 8 mm, and 13.5 mm across; 57 mm fully open). A block 'stands beside' the head when both grippers have let go of it, its 80 mm axis is within 10 degrees of vertical, its 70 mm side is within 15 degrees of the board's long axis seen from above, its lowest point is within 3 mm of the board's top, and its centre is within 25 mm of the head's centre along x. Score 0 if at any moment the head's centre was more than 8 mm from its start seen from above, its lowest point more than 10 mm above the board, or its axis more than 10 degrees from vertical (pushed, lifted or tipped, even if put back), or if at the end any block reaches more than 5 mm inside the head's outline seen from above (on, over or leaning across the head). Otherwise each side of the head scores its best block there: 0.5 if it stands beside the head with a gap of 5 mm or less (snug), 0.25 if it stands beside the head with a gap of 15 mm or less, 0 if neither; the score is the sum of the two sides, so two blocks on one side count once. Possible scores: 0, 0.25 (one block within 15 mm), 0.5 (one snug block, or a block within 15 mm on each side), 0.75 (one snug and one within 15 mm), 1.0 (both snug). The trial ends early once 1.0 has held with the head and both blocks still (under 1 cm/s and 0.5 rad/s) for 1 s; otherwise it is scored as it stands at the run limit. On a step where the grippers cannot be read, every block is taken as let go. In a real trial, the tape marks and the video show whether the head moved, a feeler gauge or ruler gives each gap, a protractor the angles, and the video whether the grippers let go.
fidelity: Rigid bodies with the simulator's default friction. The trainer is a fixed torso and neck and a loose uniform cylinder for the head (no skull shape, ears or neck joint); moving the head stands for moving the casualty's neck. The blocks are uniform rigid boxes (the foam does not compress, no ear holes). Straps are not simulated: the trial ends with the blocks placed and let go. Gripper heading is not read, so each finger zone is round.
reset_notes: Stand the head back on its tape marks on the board, centred at x 20.0 cm, y 0, axis vertical. Stand the two blocks upright on their marks on the table, 70 mm sides along x, centred at x 20.0 cm, y +28.0 cm and y -28.0 cm. The board, torso and neck stay fixed. Nothing is consumed.
